title: Musical Hedonia in Children: The Child-directed extended  Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire (eBMRQc)
description:
Musical reward is a multidimensional construct, extensively studied in adults using the Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire (BMRQ) and its extended version (eBMRQ). However, no validated tool currently allows children to report their own musical reward experience directly, rather than through parental proxy. We developed the eBMRQc, a child-directed adaptation of the eBMRQ comprising six items, one per subscale (Social Reward, Musical Seeking, Emotional Evocation, Mood Regulation, Sensory-Motor, Musical Absorption). In Experiment 1, 98 adults completed the adult and child versions, revealing significant correlations between corresponding total scores and subscales, as well as similar relationships with musical and dance training. In Experiment 2, 140 children (mean age 8.5 years) completed the eBMRQc using a child-adapted visual response scale, and performed a beat-alignment task. Children understood the questions, and showed variability across subscales. eBMRQc scores were unrelated to beat-alignment performance, suggesting that links 
between musical reward and rhythmic ability may depend on additional factors. Findings show feasibility and conceptual validity of the eBMRQc as a self-report questionnaire of musical reward in elementary school-aged children. The eBMRQc may also be used as a brief assessment tool for adults and open new avenues for studying musical reward development and its relationships with individual differences.

title: Capacity Limits in Cognitive Processing Reflect the Curse of Generalization
description:
The striking constraints of some human cognitive processes stand in stark contrast
to the near limitless capability of others. While we can acquire and flexibly use vast amounts
of information, the amount we can process at any one time is often stiflingly limited: for
example the number of items we can hold in working memory or the number of tasks that can
be performed at once. Here, we integrate ideas from information theory, cognitive science,
and neuroscience to offer a unified account of why processing is often so limited. We argue
that this reflects a fundamental tradeoff between generalization—how effectively existing
representations can be used in novel settings—and how many distinct representations can
be processed in parallel. Representations that best promote strong forms of generalization
— a characteristically human cognitive strength — come at the expense of surprisingly
strict limits in the number of items that can be processed at once, an equally characteristic
human weakness. We refer to this as the “curse of generalization.” We formulate this first in
information-theoretic terms, and then in process models, including a neural network model
of classic tasks used to demonstrate strict limits in human processing capacity. This tension
offers a potential explanation for a range of phenomena — from performance on the tasks on
which we focus, to representational learning and skill acquisition more broadly — as well
as the performance of modern machine learning architectures that exhibit generalization
capabilities comparable to humans.

title: Sex and Ethnicity Disparities in Autism Diagnosis: Population-Level Findings from Linked Health and Education Data
description: There is limited robust population level evidence on the widely reported disparities in autism diagnosis by sex and ethnicity. Universal measures of school readiness, particularly the domains measuring social and emotional development, have been proposed as early indicators of developmental need, but whether the disparities in formal diagnoses across demographic groups are reflected in these population-level measures remains unclear. This study examined how sex, ethnicity, and their intersection were associated with the frequency and timing of childhood autism diagnoses and whether school readiness measures were associated with subsequent diagnosis across demographic groups. Linked health and education records for 55,054 children from a Northwest District of England were analysed using Poisson regression. Children from minoritised ethnic backgrounds and females were less like to receive an autism diagnosis and experienced significantly longer times to diagnosis than males and White British children. South Asian heritage females showed the greatest disadvantage. These patterns were not reflected across distributions of school readiness scores, suggesting diagnostic disparities by sex and ethnicity may reflect structural inequalities within identification pathways rather than true differences in underlying need. Developmental differences are evident and measurable by age five across demographics, highlighting the opportunity for earlier identification and support.

title: Statistical learning and reading: sensitivity to letter co-occurrence statistics in eye movements across languages
description: The connection between reading and statistical learning has been heavily studied recently; letters and other linguistic units co-occur in very informative ways, and there is strong evidence now that we take advantage of that information. However, empirical studies on n-gram effects have yielded mixed results, likely due to inconsistencies regarding metrics, units and the specific characteristics of the languages investigated. In this study, we assessed the impact of several bigram, trigram, and quadrigram statistics in English, German, Spanish and Italian, to see whether sensitivity to n-grams emerges and whether it changes as a function of orthographic depth, morphological complexity, and word length. To this end, we employed the data of the Multilingual Eye-tracking corpus (MECO, Siegelmann et al., 2022). We performed separate type- and token-based analyses in each language, using the components issued by Principal Component Analyses -- for first-of-many fixation duration, single fixation duration and gaze duration. We then ran a replication with new eye-tracking data published in the second wave of MECO (Siegelmann et al., 2025), to check whether our first findings would be stable across samples. Overall, we show clear evidence for sensitivity to n-gram statistics, reinforcing the view that some form of statistical learning contributes to reading. We also see no evidence for a privileged role of bigrams across languages, against a common assumption in reading models. Finally, cross-linguistic comparisons did not show a systematic effect of orthographic depth, morphological complexity, or word length, suggesting that sensitivity to the frequency of letter co-occurrence is a general driver of reading skills.

title: Integration of a Mixed Reality Game With Innovative Eye Tracking System and Breathing Biofeedback for Adolescent Basketball Players: a Formative Usability Study
description: A Mixed Reality (MR) breathing biofeedback game with eye-tracking was developed from January 2025 to September 2025 for adolescent basketball players. Rather than drawing conclusions regarding effectiveness, this study focuses on the development, design and formative usability evaluation of this prototype across multiple stakeholder groups, and does not claim a novel algorithmic contribution yet. MR refers to the integration of virtual objects within the physical environment, enabling real-time interaction with digital components. Participants were instructed to follow a diaphragmatic breathing pattern of six breaths per minute while simultaneously performing attentional exercises via the eye-tracking functions featured in the head-mounted display. To monitor the quality and pace of the breathing pattern, a simple controller-based biofeedback mechanism was developed by manually placing the controller on the abdominal area. Twelve adolescent basketball players, three basketball trainers and four psychology experts participated in a formative usability session to assess the current iteration of the game and its readiness for a larger pilot study. A mixed methods analysis was conducted using quantitative Likert scale scores and qualitative thematic analysis. The survey findings showed good overall acceptance across all groups for content and technical appropriateness (M=4.04; SD=0.75). However, qualitative analysis of the emerging themes showed mixed findings, with 54% positive valence and six areas identified for further improvement: 1) instruction clarity, 2) session length optimization, 3) technical stability, 4) visual design, 5) theoretical validation, and 6) practical implementation. These formative findings identify key technical, instructional, and implementation-related refinements required before evaluation in a larger trial.
